cloze.title: 原文选词填空
cloze.instruction: 从词库中选择合适的词填入空白，每词使用一次，保留原文词形。大小写不影响判分。

parts.text: Its complex wetlands support migratory wading birds, numerous fish species and the Arabian collared kingfisher, a

found only in this region. Young green turtles also swim through its winding mangrove channels.

Although the wetland is now protected and recognised as a Ramsar site, a type of conservation designation for any internationally important wetlands, it has not

human development. The city of Kalba surrounds much of the site, and a large human-made basin (like a lagoon) was built alongside the natural mangroves in the early 2000s as a proposed recreational and commercial waterfront. The basin was never used for its

recreational purposes and has since been incorporated into the protected area.

To understand how young turtles use this unusual landscape alongside the natural mangrove channels, EPAA staff carefully captured nine juvenile green turtles in 2019 and

satellite tags to their shells using a specialist, harmless resin. After the turtles were released, the tags allowed us to follow their movements.

After seven months and over 2,800 satellite

the results were clear. We found Kalba’s wetlands were a critical habitat for all nine turtles. They generally stayed within just 2 miles of the wetland entrance and spent more than 80% of their tracked time inside the marine protected area’s boundary.

Basin benefits

One of the more surprising findings was the

of the human-made basin (similar to a saltwater lagoon extending from the mangroves). The turtles were around five times more likely to be found there than elsewhere in the wetland, and 77% of their core-use areas were

within it.

We cannot say for certain why the turtles favoured the basin. One possibility is that algae growing on its floor provides food, while its enclosed layout may offer shelter from larger predators. Whatever the explanation, the findings suggest that

can make use of human-modified environments.

However, this is no substitute for protecting natural habitats. Where coastal environments are modified or restored, designs that retain natural habitats, maintain connections between them and preserve the

processes they depend on may offer the greatest benefits for wildlife.

One turtle eventually embarked on a very different journey. After remaining in the wetland for 93 days, it travelled over 500 miles to Masirah Island in neighbouring Oman. This
journey highlights how a small coastal wetland can be important to young turtles before they move into wider waters.
